title: KV memory reclaimer: simulator & heuristics playbook
body:
Summary:

This doc captures a prototype design and experimental plan for a conservative, low-latency KV cache reclaimer that targets slabless pools and mitigates fragmentation while preserving tail latency SLOs. It accompanies a lightweight simulator we can use to iterate heuristics before touching production runtime code.

Motivation:

Current allocator/eviction designs in serving-runtime are tuned around slab-based allocators and workload modes with stable object size distributions (short prompt continuations). We observe two operational pain points: (1) persistent external fragmentation when object sizes vary (beam/hallucination tokens + extended dialogues), and (2) background compaction that spikes CPU/GPU memory pressure causing tail latency blips.

Goals (non-exhaustive):
- Reduce long-term external fragmentation across mixed size workloads by 30–60% in simulation under representative traces.
- Keep foreground path (request-critical allocations/reads) lock-free or wait-free under normal load.
- Provide a throttled background reclaimer that can make progress without violating percentiles (p99/p999) SLAs.
- Design observability signals that let ops decide when to trigger aggressive compaction or fall back to lower-quality models.

Design Overview:

Core idea: sliding-window reclaimer + incremental relocation.
- Keep allocator slabless (variable-size chunks) to avoid fixed-bucket waste at the cost of fragmentation risk.
- Maintain a lightweight physical-page map (page-state bitmap + occupancy traces) to identify candidate regions for relocation.
- Use a sliding-window hotness estimator (approximate LRU with exponential decay) to separate truly cold KV entries from transiently inactive ones.
- Run relocation in small chunks (page-granular moves) so each compaction step has bounded CPU and GPU memory overhead.

Key data structures (simplified):
- page_state[]: byte per page {FREE, PARTIAL, FULL, RELOCATING} stored in a compact array per arena.
- region_summary: rolling summaries of occupancy and average object size for every 4–16 consecutive pages. Updated amortized on allocation/free.
- hotness_counters: per-key approximate decayed counter (8-bit) stored in the KV metadata; updated on access. Periodically decayed by a background tick.
- relocation_log: circular buffer tracking in-flight relocations for crash-recovery and safe reclamation.

Reclaimer policy (high level):
1) Sampling: periodically sample region_summary to rank regions by fragmentation score = (w1 * free_ratio) + (w2 * size_variance) - (w3 * coldness_score). We tune w1..w3 in the simulator.
2) Candidate selection: pick highest fragmentation score regions whose hotness histogram shows >X% entries below cold threshold.
3) Incremental relocation: for each candidate region, copy live KV entries into fresh allocations in other arenas (prefer same NUMA domain where possible), update pointers in-place using an epoch/sequence number to avoid races. Mark source pages RELOCATING until move completes.
4) Commit: once a small batch (e.g., 8–64 objects or up to 4 pages) is moved and atomic metadata swapped, mark pages FREE and update page_state.
5) Backoff: if allocation pressure or tail latency rises above thresholds, throttle relocation frequency and shrink batch size.

NUMA considerations and placement rules:
- Maintain separate arenas per NUMA node. Reclamation prefers intra-node relocations to minimize remote allocation penalties.
- If underutilized nodes exist, allow cross-node relocations but only at low-priority background levels.
- Track remote allocation ratio as a KPI; simulator scenarios include spikes in remote allocations to validate trade-offs.

Fragmentation metrics we'll compute in simulator and expose in runtime metrics:
- external_fragmentation_pct = 1 - (largest_contiguous_free / total_free)
- internal_waste_ratio = sum(allocated_space - object_payload) / sum(allocated_space)
- occupancy_entropy = Shannon entropy of object-size distribution across pages (high entropy => harder to pack)
- relocation_amortized_cost = cycles_per_token_moved + incremental latency impact per relocation batch

Hotness estimator and eviction integration:
- Hotness counters are lightweight (8-bit saturating) and biased to recent accesses. Eviction policy uses a two-stage approach: 1) prefer free list and simple LRU for extremely hot traffic; 2) when under fragmentation pressure, consult region fragmentation + hotness histogram to prefer evict-move (relocate then free) vs direct eviction.
- Edge case: large single objects (>> page size) are pinned and excluded from relocation unless explicitly compacted during maintenance windows.

Simulator design notes:
- Purpose: iterate on scoring function and throttling parameters without risking production instabilities.
- Input traces: sample of production allocation/free traces (anonymized), synthetic mixes (chatty, embedding-batch, long-continuations), and stress cases (many large one-off allocations).
- Core components: allocator model, page_state model, hotness model, background worker model, and a simple tail-latency cost model that converts incremental CPU/GPU work into latency percentiles using measured shapes from real infra.
- Output per run: fragmentation metrics over time, relocation bytes, CPU cycles consumed by reclaimer, percentage of remote allocations, and simulated p50/p95/p99 latency impact.

Experiments to run (priority):
- Baseline: current allocator behavior (no relocation) across three traces.
- Heuristic sweep: vary weights w1..w3 and cold threshold; measure fragmentation reduction vs background CPU cost.
- Batch sizing: measure effect of relocation_batches = {1,4,16,64} objects and page_batch = {1,2,4} on p99 tail latency.
- NUMA placement: enable/disable cross-node relocations and measure remote allocation ratios and latency trade-offs.
- Emergency fallback: simulate sudden load spike during compaction and validate backoff logic prevents p999 SLA violations.

Observability and runtime knobs:
- Metrics to emit: region_fragmentation_score{arena,region}, page_state_counts{FREE,RELOCATING,PARTIAL,USED}, relocation_bytes_total, relocation_batches, hotness_deciles, external_fragmentation_pct, internal_waste_ratio.
- Tracing: emit relocation spans with tags: arena, pages_touched, moved_objects, cpu_ms, backpressure_reason.
- Runtime knobs: relocation_enabled, max_batch_objects, max_batch_pages, relocation_cpu_budget_pct, cold_threshold, prefer_same_numa.

Safety, consistency, and crash recovery:
- Movements are done with two-phase pointer swap protected by sequence numbers in metadata. Readers always validate sequence numbers and retry on mismatch. This ensures no stale pointers are returned even if a relocation is in progress.
- relocation_log is persisted to a short-lived journal in memory; on process restart we scan any incomplete relocations and either finish or roll back depending on sequence state. Simulator models stuttery crashes to ensure safety invariants are respected.

Integration with scheduler/kernels:
- Reclaimer should expose scheduling hints to the runtime scheduler: preferred CPU cores (background pool), affinity to NUMA nodes, and soft-priority bands.
- For entries that are queued for relocation and then hot-accessed, the hotness update moves them back up and cancels relocation; such cancellations are cheap because relocation is incremental and visibility is via the relocation_log.
- Kernel-level considerations: avoid calling heavy GPU kernels during relocation windows; relocation should prefer host-side copy into device-mapped buffers only when moving hot KV entries used by GPU inference.

Open questions / trade-offs to validate in sim:
- Is per-key hotness stored inline too expensive memory-wise at scale? Alternative: bloom sketches per region + sampled key-level counters.
- How aggressive should cross-NUMA relocations be when they reduce fragmentation but increase remote allocation tails?
- Optimal decay constant for hotness (seconds vs number of accesses) for mixed interactive+batch traffic.

Migration plan (if simulator results look good):
1) Add metrics and read-only page_state snapshots to prod (safe, opt-in).
2) Deploy small-scale pilot on a canary fleet with relocation_enabled=false but emitting simulated relocation decisions to verify scoring distribution.
3) Enable relocation_enabled with conservative defaults and strong throttling (cpu_budget_pct 2–5%).
4) Gradually increase batch sizes and allow inter-node relocations with a phased rollout and rollback hooks.

Action items (next 4 weeks):
- Asha: finalize simulator harness and commit baseline traces (JIRA-KV-492).
- Diego: prototype page_state and region summaries in simulator.
- Mira: define observability schema and mapping to Console dashboards; draft alert thresholds.
- Omar: run initial heuristic sweep and produce a short results note.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally pragmatic: small, repeatable relocation steps and a strong simulator-first philosophy to avoid surprising production behavior.
- Please call out any missing safety scenarios or workloads we should add to trace corpus.

References and prior art:
- Bloom & reservoir sketching approaches for hotness estimation (see linked_artifacts).
- Papers on incremental compaction and object relocation in memory managers (we should gather a short bibliography if this becomes a formal spec).

End of document.
